About me

Six things I've been wrong about, and what each one cost.

01

Copy cannot fix architecture.

I shipped clearer loading copy once — honest time estimates, warmer tone, the works. It moved nothing. When the interaction is confusing, words are a bandage on a broken mental model. "Let's reword it" now reads to me as a signal we haven't found the problem yet.

02

The playbook is a hypothesis.

Every competitor filled onboarding waits with demo data. Every pattern library agreed. Two weeks of recordings said the demo data was the problem. Benchmarking tells you what an industry believes — not what's true for your users.

03

A design system is an agreement.

Tokens and components are the visible part. The real work is getting 15 engineers, several PMs and a CEO to trust one source of truth — and to feel respected rather than overridden while you consolidate work they already shipped.

04

Trust lives in small placements.

Where the login wall sits. Whether a price is visible before commitment. Which parent brand mark you see first. In a financial product these aren't UI decisions — they're the product.

05

Say what the numbers can't prove.

Session recordings gave me behavioural certainty and statistical ambiguity. Those aren't the same thing, and pretending they are is how design loses credibility with engineering and data. Every result here is labelled with how confidently it was measured.

06

I came to this from engineering.

Four years at Larsen & Toubro running cross-functional delivery and building Power BI dashboards before I opened Figma. It's why I reach for behavioural data before a canvas, and why engineering constraints read as inputs rather than obstacles.

Case 01 · Bloom Analytics

How blocking access improved retention

50 merchants installed in two weeks. 13–15 came back. Most left mid-sync, during a 7–30 minute wait that every competitor was filling with demo data.

Shopify analytics SaaS Senior Product Designer 28% → 48% second-visit rate
RoleSenior Product Designer — research, IA, interaction, validation
Team1 designer, 1 PM, small engineering team
MethodsPostHog session analysis · competitive audit · iterative shipping
ConfidenceDirectional — behavioural evidence, no A/B infrastructure
The number that started it

Bloom consolidates Shopify store data, ad platforms and operational costs into one view. It only becomes valuable once a merchant's data is connected — and that connection takes 7 to 30 minutes.

In a two-week tracking window: 50 installs, 13–15 second visits. A 28% return rate, with most of the loss happening while the sync was still running.

What the recordings showed

The obvious diagnosis was that the wait was too long, so make it feel shorter. That logic points straight at demo data and feature tours. We tried it; it made things worse. So I watched every new install in PostHog for two weeks and found the same sequence every time.

0–2 minExcitement

Merchants explore, click into reports, engage. Everything works as intended.

2–5 minConfusion, not boredom

Sync still running. Numbers don't match their store. The demo data looks real at a glance, then clearly isn't. They stop trusting the screen.

5–7 min +Abandonment

Most close the app. Most never return — not because the wait was long, but because they couldn't tell what was real.

I audited HubSpot, Mailchimp, BeProfit, TrueProfit, Lifetimely and Polar Analytics. None had solved it cleanly — they either showed demo data (same confusion) or showed nothing (faster abandonment). The audit told me what the industry believed. The recordings told me what was happening.

The problem wasn't the wait. It was the uncertainty.

Merchants didn't know what was real, what was demo, how long remained, or whether something had broken. In that state no amount of interesting content helps — the information architecture itself was the failure.

Three iterations, two failures
Iteration 01 — Failed Full access, demo data

Matched every competitor. Merchants mistook demo figures for their own, found the mismatch, left frustrated.

Return rate unchanged (~28%)
Iteration 02 — Failed Better loading copy

Explained the sync, gave estimates, warmer tone. Merchants acknowledged the wait and stayed frustrated by the mixed-data experience underneath it.

No measurable change
Iteration 03 — Shipped Block the app entirely

Replaced the product with a dedicated sync experience: visible stages, opt-in demo, cost setup, email on completion.

28% → 48% second-visit rate
What iteration 2 cost me

A full sprint writing better words for a screen whose structure was the problem. It's the most useful failure of my career so far — I now push back hard whenever a team's answer to a confusing flow is a rewrite.

The counterintuitive fix

Instead of giving merchants more to explore during the sync, I blocked access to the main app and replaced it with a dedicated sync experience. That breaks the rule everyone repeats — never show a loading screen when you could show content. But the "content" was what was driving people away.

01
Stage-by-stage sync visualisation

A real progress model, not a spinner: connecting Shopify, collecting orders and ad cost, crunching numbers, building your dashboard. Merchants could see where they were and what remained. Uncertainty was the enemy, so I attacked it directly.

02
Demo access, clearly separated

A banner offering "explore a demo account while you wait" — optional, labelled, entered by choice. The difference from iteration 1 is consent: merchants knew which world they were standing in.

03
A productive wait

I resequenced the sync so product data landed first, letting merchants enter COGS and shipping costs while the rest loaded. Passive waiting became active setup — and they reached their first dashboard having already improved its accuracy.

04
Email on completion

Removed the pressure to keep the tab open, and killed the "I'll check later and forget" pattern that was quietly destroying second visits.

28→48%
Second- and third-visit rate across comparable install windows
~15→~24
Returning merchants per 50 installs
Sustained
Held across later install cohorts — not a one-time spike
What I'd measure if I ran this again

The honest limitation is measurement rigour. PostHog gave us behavioural evidence, not statistical confidence, and we were a small team without the infrastructure for a clean A/B test. Starting over I'd instrument four things from day one: sync completion rate, time-to-first-meaningful-action after sync, second-visit rate at 24 hours and 7 days, and feature-adoption depth on that second visit. The insight was strong; the instrumentation wasn't built to match it.

What this changed about how I think

The most important decision here wasn't a UI decision. It was choosing to trust two weeks of behavioural evidence over an industry-wide consensus. Senior work is often knowing when the playbook is describing a different problem than the one in front of you.

Case 02 · Pay with Ring

One button, seven ways

10 million downloads. Seven visual variants of the same button. Four type scales in onboarding alone. Growth had quietly turned into debt — and in a lending product, inconsistency reads as instability.

Consumer fintech · India Sole designer, 1 year UX Design Awards Berlin 2024 nominee
RoleSole designer — research, system architecture, components, documentation
Scale15+ engineers, multiple feature teams, 10M+ downloads
DurationOne year to measurable velocity change
ConfidenceTeam-reported velocity + product analytics on onboarding
A problem hiding inside a growth story

From outside, Ring looked like a success — UPI, credit, bill payments, competing with Paytm and Google Pay. From inside it felt like several products stitched together. Multiple verticals, multiple designers, parallel feature teams. Nobody had done anything wrong; the debt was cumulative.

For a consumer lending product this isn't a design-quality complaint. Inconsistency erodes trust, and trust is the product.

Weeks of research before opening Figma
01
User interviews & personas

Three segments with meaningfully different needs. What they shared: they had to trust the product immediately, often in a high-stress financial moment.

02
Stakeholder interviews — CTO, CEO, Marketing, PM

A shared super-app ambition, no shared visual language. The CTO's concern was delivery speed; the CEO's was brand stickiness. A design system answered both — which is how I got the mandate.

03
UI audit

Every component catalogued. One button, seven variants. Four type scales in onboarding. No documented colour logic. Not a style problem — compounding technical and experience debt.

04
Competitive benchmarking

OneCard, Google Pay, PhonePe, Simple. Products that feel trustworthy use restraint and repetition. Predictability is the trust mechanism.

StudentsSmall, frequent credit for month-end gaps
Daily-wage earnersIrregular income, forgiving repayment moments
Kirana ownersWorking capital, high-frequency transactions
The decision that defined the system

Early on: build the minimal, safe, neutral system that is the standard fintech playbook — or build something bold and differentiated.

The safe choice had real logic behind it; minimalism signals professionalism. But Ring's users are young, underserved and mobile-first, and they didn't need another clinical interface. The bold direction tested better in validation, differentiated Ring visually, and gave the brand a reason to be remembered. I argued it with the research behind it rather than a moodboard — which is why the decision survived a leadership change and a year of execution.

How it was built
01
Audit & inventory

Components documented, redundancies mapped, gaps named. As much for credibility as correctness — we weren't discarding engineering's work, we were consolidating it.

02
Atomic build

Atoms (tokens, type scale, spacing, icons) → molecules (buttons, inputs, cards) → organisms (navigation, onboarding templates, repayment flows). Starting at atoms meant every decision in a template traced back to a token.

03
Weekly design–engineering syncs

A Figma walkthrough with engineering every week for the length of the build, instead of specs over a wall. It removed most interpretation ambiguity — and because engineers understood the intent, their edge-case decisions got better too.

04
Documentation that outlives me

Figma plus ZeroHeight: every component with usage guidelines, states, accessibility notes and do/don't examples.

+62%
Improvement in onboarding completion
3×
Faster design→engineering handoff
~70%
Reduction in design time for new features
15+
Engineers shipping from one source of truth
How these were measured

The velocity numbers weren't targets we set at the start — they're what we observed comparing delivery cadence before and after adoption, reported by engineering leads. The onboarding figure came from product analytics. I'd treat the first three as strong directional evidence from a team that had every reason to be sceptical, not as controlled measurement.

A design system isn't a component library. It's an agreement.

The technical work is the visible part. The real work was alignment: getting 15+ engineers, several PMs and a CEO with a super-app vision to trust a single source of truth. That took research to justify a bold direction, weekly syncs to keep engineering bought in, and an audit that made the existing team feel respected rather than overridden.

The system is still running. That's the metric I'm proudest of.

Case 03 · Way.id

Designing trust back into insurance

A Prudential joint venture with traffic and almost no conversions. The app looked like it didn't trust its own users — so users didn't trust it back.

Prudential × PFI Mega Life · Indonesia Sole designer, 4 months 6 of 6 features shipped
RoleSole designer — end-to-end UX and UI, research through handoff
ContextServing Indonesia's under-40, largely uninsured market
Duration4 months
ConfidenceQualitative — post-launch user and stakeholder feedback
The starting point

Poor navigation buried key information. Product cards showed no pricing clarity. The login wall appeared only when someone tapped "Buy now" — the worst possible moment for friction. And the visual design carried none of Prudential's hard-earned credibility.

Three parallel diagnoses

A design audit mapped every flow against drop-off and named the login interruption as the single biggest friction moment — users who had invested time exploring were treated like strangers at the point of commitment, and most didn't return.

Interviews with prospective customers, sales agents and internal stakeholders found the pattern underneath: people didn't doubt insurance as a concept. They doubted this app. It felt informal for a financial product.

Benchmarking against Lemonade, Digit, PasarPolis, Sun Life and Allianz gave the clearest insight of the project: apps that lead with transparency — visible pricing, clear benefit summaries, calculators before commitment — convert significantly better than those hiding details behind a contact form.

Six changes, all shipped
01
Early login

Moved authentication to the start of the session rather than the point of purchase. Users who log in early are already invested; walling off engaged users at "Buy now" was the most common abandonment trigger we found. One moment moved, one whole failure mode gone.

02
Premium calculator

The single most-requested feature in interviews. People weren't afraid of insurance — they were afraid of not knowing what they were committing to. Showing coverage ranges and estimated premiums before agent contact turned a high-anxiety decision into an exploratory one.

03
Redesigned product cards

Benefits, coverage amount and premium estimate at a glance. All three previously required drilling in; now comparison happens in the listing view, where comparison actually occurs.

04
Meli — AI assistant

A conversational path for people not ready to navigate a catalogue. Built for the Gen Z segment who expect chat-first interfaces, guiding users to a category through questions instead of menus.

05
Navigation & IA overhaul

Flattened the hierarchy so policy details, claims and support sit within two taps. The previous structure buried critical paths three and four levels deep.

06
Visual design anchored to Prudential

Colour, typography and component language re-anchored to the parent brand — putting 170+ years of accumulated trust to work instead of leaving it on the shelf.

What I'd do differently

The premium calculator shipped without real-time rate data — ranges, not live quotes. That was an engineering constraint we accepted to hit the timeline, and I'd push harder now to either integrate live rates or set a much clearer expectation about estimate versus actual. A user who gets a materially different number from an agent afterwards loses exactly the trust the project was built to create.

Outcome

All six features went live. Post-launch feedback converged on two themes: navigation felt noticeably faster and more intuitive, and the product finally felt trustworthy. Stakeholders specifically noted it now felt appropriate for a financial product of Prudential's standing.

Insurance is a trust product. Every placement is a trust signal.

Where the login appears. Whether the price is visible. Which brand marks you see first. The work here wasn't making the app look modern — it was making people feel safe enough to start a financial relationship.
